t: Minimum Operations to Make Array Equal II — Difference Arithmetic
o: Each operation adds k to one element and subtracts k from another, so the total sum of nums1 never changes, and every element changes by multiples of k. Define d_i = nums2[i] - nums1[i]. We need every d_i divisible by k (when k > 0), positive and negative totals to cancel, and the operation count equals (total absolute adjustment)/k divided by 2 since one operation fixes +k on one side and -k on another simultaneously. Example 1: diffs are [-3,0,6,-3]; positives sum 6, negatives 6, ops = 6/3 / 2 = 2. Example 2 fails divisibility, hence -1. If k = 0 no element can change, so the answer is 0 iff arrays already match. Constraints up to 1e5 demand an O(n) formula, not simulation.
k: One operation simultaneously resolves +k of surplus and -k of deficit, so the answer is sum of positive diffs divided by k, halved.
Feasibility requires: sum of diffs = 0, every diff divisible by k (k > 0), or k = 0 with identical arrays.

a.i: Compute all diffs. Accumulate positive adjustments P and negative adjustments N. If P != N the sums can't match (-1). If k == 0, success only when P == 0. Otherwise each diff must be divisible by k and the answer is P/k operations (each operation covers one unit of +k and one of -k, so P/k counts both halves at once).
s: Build diff array d_i = nums2[i] - nums1[i].
Sum positive parts into P and negative parts into N.
If P != N return -1. If k == 0 return 0 if P == 0 else -1.
If any d_i % k != 0 return -1; otherwise return P // k.
a.t: O(n) — three linear passes over the arrays

w: This formula is the interview answer; brute-force simulation is unnecessary. Watch the k = 0 edge case (division by zero) and use 64-bit sums since values reach 1e9 with n = 1e5. Follow-ups: minimize operations if an operation could add k to i and subtract k from j with i = j allowed (then answer unchanged), or if only increments were allowed (feasibility changes completely).
